title: Rate and mechanism of maximal oxygen consumption decline with aging: implications for exercise training
population: Review of cross-sectional and longitudinal studies of VO2max decline in sedentary and athletic men and women
findings: Current evidence supports a 10% per decade decline in VO2max in men and women regardless of activity level.

High-intensity exercise may reduce the loss by up to 50% in young and middle-aged men, but not older men, if maintained long term; middle-aged and older women do not appear able to reduce loss below 10% per decade (possibly related to estrogen status).
Maintaining high-intensity training seems limited to approximately one decade at best and to a select few; training maintenance becomes more difficult with advancing age.
VO2max loss is non-linear, associated with declines in physical activity (athletes show a non-linear decline on reducing or ceasing training; also non-linear after 70).

The decline is due to central and peripheral changes, primarily reductions in HRmax and lean body mass; training does not influence the HRmax decline while lean mass can be partly maintained, so strength training is recommended.
limitations: Narrative review; the 10% per decade figure mixes cross-sectional and limited longitudinal data and is challenged by later longitudinal data (Letnes 2020 reports much lower decline in the 20s-40s and higher after 70).
implications: Use about 10% per decade (about 1% per year) only as an upper-range long-term VO2max/threshold-speed decline assumption for multi-year projection, not a within-block adjustment.
Strength training for masters to preserve lean mass is recommended by the review; the specific frequency (1-2 sessions per week) is an engine default, not a figure from the paper.
Do not assume a runner can sustain high-intensity density indefinitely; monitor tolerance over multi-year plans rather than hard-coding a deload schedule.

verification.notes: Crossref and Europe PMC abstract match. Added the non-linear-decline and estrogen statements; removed the researcher's invented '1-2 sessions' and 'deload' attributions.
